item.title: NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates Molecular Dynamics Simulations

🔍 Overview

Molecular dynamics (MD) is an indispensable tool across physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science.

🧩 How it works

Owing to its arithmetic structure, particularly the parallel evaluation of many atom-pair interactions, MD codes were among the first to be ported to run on GPUs.

However, as GPUs evolve, optimizing kernels and ensuring compatibility across heterogeneous hardware have become more difficult than ever for many MD engine developers.

⚙️ Key details

NVIDIA cuPotential is a focused library designed for molecular dynamics, addressing these challenges.

🚀 Availability

Building the cuPotential runtime and plugin for OpenMM requires:

• Linux x86-64 with a supported NVIDIA GPU

• An installed NVIDIA driver compatible with CUDA 13.1

• Conda or Micromamba installed and initialized for your shell

• A clone of the cuPotential repository from the NVIDIA/cuPotential GitHub repo

💡 Why it matters

The cuPotential OpenMM plugin provides replacements for the OpenMM nonbonded force, Langevin integrator, and Monte Carlo barostat, enabling seamless drop-in replacements with minimal changes to the user’s code.

💻 Using cuPotential with OpenMM

The cuPotential OpenMM plugin provides replacements for the OpenMM nonbonded force, Langevin integrator, and Monte Carlo barostat.

📊 Performance

The cuPotential arm uses its own force and integrator, plus its barostat for NPT, resulting in a reported speedup.

📊 Key Features

• Modular primitives with a C API

• Direct space and reciprocal space utilities

• Cutoff-based interaction evaluators and charge spreading functions

📊 Model Variants

• cuPotential provides a plugin specifically for OpenMM

📊 Capabilities

• Acceleration of workloads on heterogeneous hardware

• Seamless drop-in replacements with minimal changes to the user’s code

#AI #MachineLearning #GPUAcceleration

Source: Accelerate Molecular Dynamics Simulations with Accurate, Flexible Primitives Using NVIDIA cuPotential | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: OpenScreen: Free, Open-Source Screen Recording App with AI Editing
item.description:
OpenScreen: Free, Open-Source Screen Recording App with AI Editing

OpenScreen is a new open-source desktop application that turns raw screen recordings into polished demos without watermarks or subscriptions. It supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, offering features like AI-powered editing, automatic captions, and GPU-accelerated export.

📸 What It Does

OpenScreen is designed to help users record their screen and instantly transform the result into share-ready content for platforms like YouTube, X, Reddit, or documentation sites.

Key capabilities include:

  • Record a specific window or your entire screen
  • Capture both microphone and system audio
  • Webcam overlay with picture-in-picture mode
  • Auto and manual zooms with adjustable settings
  • Custom cursor size, smoothing, and click effects
  • Automatic on-device captions with offline transcription
  • An AI editing assistant that applies changes from natural language descriptions
  • Support for multiple background options including wallpapers and gradients
  • Motion blur and per-segment speed control on the timeline
  • Text, arrow, and image annotations with animation presets
  • Timeline snapping guides and audio waveform visualization
  • Export to MP4 or GIF with GPU-accelerated rendering (Metal, D3D11, Vulkan)

⚙️ Key Details

Feature Description
Licensing MIT License, 100% free for personal and commercial use
Platforms Windows, macOS, Linux
AI Assistant Works with Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Mistral, OpenRouter, MiniMax, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
CLI Support Headless recording, JSON editing, and rendering via command line
Caption Languages Arabic, Czech, English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, Turkish, Vietnamese, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese

Development started with Siddharth Vaddem, who archived the original repository after v1.5.0 before moving development to a new repository under the same name and MIT license. The project remains actively maintained, though users should expect rough edges and occasional breaking changes to the project format and CLI.

#OpenSource #ScreenRecording #AIEditing #GPUAcceleration #CLI
